items.followUp: Write down any four properties of a colloidal solution.

rubric.why: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture.
rubric.description: Identify a suspension as a heterogeneous mixture.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a suspension is heterogeneous.

rubric.why: Suspension particles are large enough to be seen with the naked eye.
rubric.description: State that suspension particles are visible to the naked eye.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct statement about the visibility of the particles.

rubric.why: Suspension particles settle when the mixture is left standing.
rubric.description: State that suspension particles settle on standing.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing settling.

rubric.why: Suspension particles can be separated from the mixture by filtration.
rubric.description: State that suspension particles can be separated by filtration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying filtration as a separation method.

modelAnswer: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture.
Its particles are large enough to be seen with the naked eye.
The particles settle down when the suspension is left standing.
The particles can be separated from the mixture by filtration.

items.followUp: Explain why the first ionization energy of potassium is lower than that of calcium.

rubric.why: Sodium has one electron in its outer shell, while magnesium has two.
rubric.description: Compare the outer-shell electron configurations of sodium and magnesium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying sodium's outer-shell electron arrangement or its one outer electron.

rubric.why: Magnesium attracts its outer electrons more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove one than from sodium.
rubric.description: Explain why magnesium holds its outer electrons more strongly, giving it a higher ionization energy than sodium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct comparison of attraction or electron binding that explains sodium's lower ionization energy.

modelAnswer: Sodium has the electronic configuration 2,8,1, while magnesium has 2,8,2.
Magnesium has a greater nuclear charge and a smaller atomic radius, so its outer electrons are held more strongly; therefore, sodium has the lower ionization energy.

items.followUp: Define an ionic bond and give one example.

rubric.why: A chemical bond is an attractive force that holds atoms or ions together.
rubric.description: Define a chemical bond as an attractive force holding atoms or ions together.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the defining attractive-force and holding-together idea.

rubric.why: A correct example shows a substance containing chemical bonds.
rubric.description: Give one valid example of a substance with a chemical bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: A chemical bond is the attractive force that holds atoms or ions together in a molecule or compound.
For example, the hydrogen atoms in H₂ are held together by a chemical bond.

items.followUp: Show, using electron configurations, how Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions are formed.

rubric.why: A sodium atom loses one electron and forms a positively charged sodium ion.
rubric.description: Explain the formation of Na⁺ by loss of one electron from sodium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying the electron loss and resulting Na⁺ ion.

rubric.why: A chlorine atom gains one electron and forms a negatively charged chloride ion.
rubric.description: Explain the formation of Cl⁻ by gain of one electron by chlorine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying the electron gain and resulting Cl⁻ ion.

modelAnswer: A sodium atom loses one electron to form a sodium ion: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻.
A chlorine atom gains one electron to form a chloride ion: Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻.

items.followUp: Define diffusion of gases and give an example involving ammonia and hydrogen chloride.

rubric.why: Diffusion is the spreading and mixing of gas particles from higher to lower concentration.
rubric.description: Define diffusion of gases in terms of particle spreading from higher to lower concentration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition that describes the movement or spreading of gas particles.

rubric.why: An appropriate example shows gases spreading and mixing by diffusion.
rubric.description: Give one correct example of diffusion of gases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example.

modelAnswer: Diffusion of gases is the spreading and mixing of gas particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
For example, the smell of perfume spreads through a room by diffusion.

items.followUp: Why are gases less dense than liquids?

rubric.why: Particles in solids are generally closer together than particles in liquids, with less empty space between them.
rubric.description: Compare the packing or spacing of particles in solids and liquids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that solid particles are more closely packed or have less space between them.

rubric.why: Closer packing generally means more mass in a given volume and therefore greater density.
rubric.description: Link the closer packing of solid particles to greater density.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for connecting the particle arrangement with greater mass per unit volume or greater density.

modelAnswer: The particles in solids are packed more closely together than those in liquids, with less empty space between them.
Therefore, a given volume of a solid generally contains more mass and has a greater density.
